articles.title: The tipping point of change
articles.description: DISCUSSIONS are happening about how so many of the young protesters that rocked the Modi government recently came from families that have been faithfully voting for the right-wing prime minister. A crucial fact that seems to elude the discussants is that liberal or communist or fascist ideologues are not hatched in hatcheries. Unlike Narendra Modi, they are not ‘non-biological’ beings that gatecrash our earthly world. To begin with, it would be useful to bear in mind that the jailed left-wing student leader Umar Khalid had transcended to secular left politics from circumstances in which his father was a member of a major Muslim revivalist body. Likewise, Neha Bora, president of the pro-communist All-India Students’ Association who fasted for 23 days at the protest, tells you sans demur that she broke away from a family tradition of voting for the Muslim-baiting BJP. The flow can be in the opposite direction too. Howard Fast, as the despairing chief of the US Communist Party, famed for writing the story of Spartacus, the slave rebel of Rome, became a Buddhist seeker after abandoning Marxism. Numerous such examples abound in the Indian intellectual pantheon of progressivism and regression, which we can discuss. A scene is vivid from my childhood in which the migration to progressive politics would seem facile despite the good intentions. It was a balmy morning in Mustafabad, a village of erstwhile Shia taluqdars in the heart of Uttar Pradesh. Some young men and women in the joint family had recently got the first university degrees. Marxism was in the air in university campuses in the 1960s. That morning the tea was of just the right temperature, its bouquet flavourful. Three bespectacled young men from among the learned ones were steeped in a discussion that straddled Marx, Nehru, Josh and Neruda. The men were wrapped in embroidered woollen shawls over spotless white muslin kurta-pajama attires when the mehtrani, the woman carrying human refuse in an open reed basket, walked past. Other than putting the handkerchiefs on their faces briefly, the men remained unabashedly unperturbed in their intellectual chatter. A follower of Dalit politics would have reacted differently to the brutal absurdness of the frame. Indian communists added B.R. Ambedkar and the sickening caste angle to their class analysis grudgingly, only recently harnessing it to the dialectical quiver. These early activists had the theory but not the praxis, which would take years to arrive, or perhaps not. It’s not clear that most of the youth who defied the fierce police assault the other day had, in fact, crossed the tipping point from their social reality. Thus, it’s not even clear that most of the youth who defied the fierce police assault the other day to scare the hell out of a stubborn authoritarian government had, in fact, crossed the tipping point from their social reality. A Buddhist would call the migration nirvana — the blowing out of greed, hatred and ignorance. Collectively, the youth displayed a healthy mix of all three characteristics. When and if they reassemble it could be a different variety of mix. Arvind Kejriwal had held out a similar promise when his Aam Aadmi Party stop­ped the Hindutva juggernaut in Delhi in 2015. The ‘Modi wave’ had taken care of Maharashtra and Haryana state polls in quick succession. Kejriwal stopped the BJP chariot in Delhi. Then something equally important occurred. He rejected the offer of support from the Shahi Imam of Jama Masjid, and people were emboldened to believe that the time had come to separate religion from politics as the constitution ordains. Then in a crude display of regressive religiosity, he started holding election campaigns from Hindu temples and wooed senior voters with offers of free Hindu pilgrimages. One doesn’t have to agree with T.S. Eliot who says: “Youth is cruel and has no remorse. And smiles at situations it cannot see.” But youth is a handy demographic factor with an uncertain political trajectory. Not long ago, taking on the same Modi establishment, a courageous woman had single-handedly instigated the downfall of Modi’s minister accused of sexual transgressions. But the same charges failed to secure the conviction of a BJP muscleman. However, there again is the unforgettable instance of determined and seasoned farmers who forced the cancellation of Modi’s prized anti-farm laws. It is heartening to remember, therefore, that the Cockroach leaders have committed themselves to deter violations of citizen’s voting rights by a wayward election commission. The youth are committed to take on the hopelessly compromised corporate media that misreported the protests. Keeping company in the progressive transition of Khalid and Bora are some very eminent intellectuals of the subcontinent. Faiz Ahmed Faiz’s path from traditional Islamic education to becoming one of South Asia’s most iconic Marxist intellectuals highlights a fascinating evolution. Majro­­oh Sultanpuri was destined to become a hakim, for which he had acquired a degree. Then he turned towards left politics and endured isolation and even jail for his beliefs. I recently saw lovely pictures of Faiz’s daughters on a holiday in Sri Lanka. Had DPT been around, they would have in all likelihood been in India for he had the magic of fixing visas for all manner of progressive Pakis­tanis. Devi Prasad Tripathi came to JNU from the RSS stable. He became a staunch member of the Communist Party of India-Marxist and won the election as student union president when he was arrested and jailed during the emergency. Many political stalwarts left the RSS to become leftists and are leading critics of the Modi establishment. Kaifi Azmi became a progressive writer after early inspiration from the valour of Imam Husain. And, Iran has shown that a just battle can harness religious motifs to thwart a powerful aggressor. “ Dekhna Kaifi nishan-i-hurriyat lahraega/ Jab jahan ko azm-i-Sher-i-Karbala mil jayaega ” (‘Watch, O Kaifi, the banner of freedom shall flutter high/ Once the world finds the Lion of Karbala and joins his battle cry’). Kaifi’s pre-Marxist verses presaged the retreat of imperialism not far from the site of the students’ protest. And Iran’s left? They’re cohabiting with imperialism. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi. jawednaqvi@gmail.com Published in Dawn, August 11th, 2026

articles.title: Equal citizens
articles.description: AUG 11 occupies a special place in our history because it was on this day in 1947 that Quaid-i-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah set out what citizenship in the new state ought to mean. Addressing the Constituent Assembly, he spoke of a country in which people were free to go to their temples, mosques or other places of worship, and where religion, caste or creed would not determine their standing before the state. He insisted that citizens should enjoy equal rights, privileges and obligations, and that discrimination between communities had no place in the order Pakistan was attempting to build. These remarks formed part of a wider vision of government based on law, impartiality, protection of life and property, and the safeguarding of religious belief. It is fitting, then, that minority rights activists will gather outside Mazar-i-Quaid in Karachi today to recall that promise and demand that it be honoured. The Minority Rights March has put forward 11 demands, including stronger safeguards against forced conversions, protection from the misuse of blasphemy laws, greater political representation, removal of discriminatory material from textbooks, protection of minority properties and places of worship, and expanded access to education and employment. Organisers have also called for constitutional amendments allowing non-Muslim citizens to qualify for the offices of president and prime minister. Whether every demand commands consensus is a matter for democratic debate. But the principle from which they proceed — that citizenship should not be graded according to faith — should not be controversial in a republic that continues to invoke Jinnah as its founding authority. The delay in a written NOC for the march deserves attention. Peaceful assembly is a right, not a favour. The gap between Jinnah’s principle of equal citizenship and present realities cannot be ignored. It is especially troubling because these protections were articulated at the birth of Pakistan itself. Religious minorities continue to face mob violence, attacks on their places of worship, forced conversions and social and economic exclusion. Laws intended to protect religion have at times been weaponised through false accusations, with consequences extending far beyond the courtroom. Even where the state guarantees equality, social prejudice and institutional barriers make that guarantee fragile in practice. National Minority Rights Day must be more than a ceremonial observance. It should prompt the state to examine where law, policy and public culture continue to fall short of the standard articulated on Aug 11, 1947. Jinnah did not ask minorities to be grateful for protection; he described equal citizenship as a fundamental principle. Pakistan cannot honour that principle through speeches alone. It will honour it when every citizen, regardless of faith, can claim the same dignity, security and political belonging. Published in Dawn, August 11th, 2026

articles.title: Trump throws new tantrum as Iran makes bold demand
articles.description: President Donald Trump issued a new ultimatum for ending the Iran war as peace talks appear to have broken down. Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary demanded compensation for war damages and an end to U.S. sanctions as a condition for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, and Trump fired off a Truth Social post making the same demand to end the war he launched on Feb. 28. "I see that Representatives of the Islamic Republic of Iran are asking for compensation for the damage done to them during the last five month Military Conflict (started because, THEY WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON), even though it was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings!" Trump posted Monday afternoon. Trump called for Iran to provide compensation for a wide-ranging list of alleged misdeeds. "But it is an interesting idea because now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by General Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat," Trump posted. "Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protestors that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months." "I have instructed my representatives to put this firmly into any, and all, future negotiations ," he added. Trump claimed over the weekend that the U.S. was only "semi-negotiating" with Iran and indicated that he would allow economic pressure to build on Tehran as leverage to end the war.

articles.title: ‘Jail time’ calls surge as 'insane' right-wing AI attack ad airs in red state
articles.description: A new political attack ad against Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico left onlookers floored Monday for its use of generative artificial intelligence to depict the Texas Democrat as a doctor preparing to perform surgery on a young child. “I think using an AI version of a candidate in a political advertisement should result in jail time,” wrote D.C.-based journalist Amanda Moore Monday in a social media post on X. Put out by the American Principles Project on behalf of GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton, the ad in question depicts a young girl plucking flower petals in a grassy field before transitioning to a shot of the same girl lying in a hospital bed wearing an oxygen mask. A doctor is shown instructing the girl to “keep counting,” and is later revealed to be a GenAI-generated depiction of Talarico. A narrator in the ad can then be heard saying the following: “The trans industry preys on confused children,” almost certainly a reference to Talarico’s pro-LGBTQ positions . Max Flugrath, a Democratic political strategist, called the ad “absolutely insane,” and characterized it as a “desperate” attempt to save Paxton’s sinking campaign . “Absolutely insane to remake an ad about the threat of nuclear war to spread fake panic about the ‘trans industry,’” Flugrath wrote in a social media post on X. “They’re so desperate to make James Talarico seem extreme they need AI.” The ad appears intentionally designed to mirror a 1964 campaign ad on behalf of Lyndon B. Johnson, which also depicted a young girl in a field plucking flower petals. Where the Johnson ad differed was its second half, which warned of nuclear armageddon rather than the “trans industry.” And, while the ad may be “the Paxton campaign’s most egregious attack yet,” Mother Jones’ Sophie Hurwitz argued that history suggested it wouldn’t land with Texas voters. “The original ‘daisy girl’ ad was effective because it was able to make people afraid. But if previous attempts to remix the daisy video are anything to go by, the American Principles Project may not succeed,” Hurwitz wrote in an analysis published Sunday. “Bob Dole, in 1996, aired a version of the daisy video that concerned itself with teenage drug use. Audiences didn’t find that particularly compelling, and Dole lost. The Hillary Clinton campaign, in 2016, tracked down the actress who starred in the original video to shoot an ad for her presidential bid. Clinton lost, too. An atom bomb is terrifying because it is real, but an AI-generated three-year-old on an operating table is a manufactured threat.”

articles.title: The U.S. just had its hottest month on record
articles.description: Reproduced from NOAA ; Chart: Axios Visuals July was the hottest month on record for the contiguous U.S., per new federal data dating back to 1895. By the numbers: Last month's average temperature was 76.89°F, topping the 76.77°F mark set in July 1936. That's 3.3°F warmer than the 1901-2000 average. What they're saying: "Above-average temperatures covered the entire [continental U.S.], with all states ranking in the warmest third of their July temperature records and none ranking near or below average," NOAA's National Centers for Environmental Information said in its monthly report . The big picture: July featured a series of "heat domes" across the country that trapped warm air beneath them, fueling several extreme heat events. Researchers have found that climate change is making extreme heat events more common and more intense — but they're also linked to phenomena and patterns like El Niño. What we're watching: NOAA's Climate Prediction Center is calling for an elevated chance of above-average temperatures for most of the continental U.S. through August. It's also possible that 2026 will set a new record for the hottest year globally.
